title: Linkability of GPS location data to child identity
description: Live GPS coordinates transmitted from child's device can be linked to the child's identity through the Mobile App Backend, enabling tracking of movements and location patterns over time.
assumptions: Backend maintains association between device and child identity; GPS data is retained and accessible.

title: Identifiability of child through location data
description: GPS coordinates can be used to identify the child's home, school, and frequent locations, making the child identifiable even without explicit identifiers.
assumptions: Location data is retained and can be correlated with other information; child's routine locations are unique.

title: Unauthorized disclosure of child's location data
description: Live GPS coordinates may be disclosed to unauthorized parties through backend vulnerabilities, insider threats, or data breaches, exposing the child's real-time location.
assumptions: Backend has access controls; data is stored and transmitted over networks.

title: Excessive data collection of live GPS coordinates
description: Continuous transmission of live GPS coordinates at regular intervals may exceed what is necessary for the stated purpose, violating data minimization principles.
assumptions: Purpose of data collection is defined; less frequent or aggregated location data could suffice.

title: Potential non-compliance with child privacy regulations
description: Collection and processing of children's location data may violate regulations such as COPPA, GDPR-K, or other child-specific privacy laws requiring parental consent and data protection measures.
assumptions: Applicable privacy regulations exist; consent mechanisms are in place.
uncertainty_note: Specific regulations depend on jurisdiction and data usage purpose.

title: Unintended Location Data Disclosure to Third Parties
description: Location pings written to the Location History Store may be accessible to unauthorized third parties, resulting in implicit data disclosure beyond intended recipients.
assumptions: The Location History Store may have access controls that are insufficient or may be breached; location data may be shared with third parties without explicit consent.
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 based on context [5] about data disclosure; the exact threat-tree node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Linkability of Location History to Individual Identity
description: Stored location history can be linked to identify specific individuals by correlating location patterns with other data sources or by tracking movement over time.
assumptions: Location data contains sufficient granularity to enable re-identification; additional data sources may exist for correlation.
uncertainty_note: Using L.1.1 as a reasonable node for linkability threats; context [4] confirms L is applicable at Process→DataStore.

title: Identifiability of Individuals from Location Data
description: Location pings can directly identify individuals by revealing their physical presence at specific times and places, potentially exposing sensitive personal information.
assumptions: Location data is precise enough to identify individuals; individuals may not be aware their location is being stored.
uncertainty_note: Using I.1.1 as a reasonable node for identifiability threats; context [4] confirms I is applicable at Process→DataStore.

title: Potential Regulatory Non-Compliance for Location Data Collection
description: Storing location history may violate privacy regulations (e.g., GDPR, CCPA) if proper consent mechanisms, data minimization, or retention policies are not implemented.
assumptions: Location data is considered personal data under applicable regulations; consent and data protection measures may be inadequate.
uncertainty_note: Using Nc.1.1 as a reasonable node for non-compliance threats; context [4] confirms Nc is applicable at Process→DataStore.

title: Linkability of Geofencing Notifications
description: The arrival/departure notifications could be linked across multiple events to reconstruct the child's movement patterns and location history, potentially revealing sensitive behavioral information about zone usage.
assumptions: Notifications are timestamped and contain identifiable information that can be correlated across events.
uncertainty_note: Tree node L.1.1 is a general linkability node; specific geofencing context may warrant more granular analysis.

title: Identification of Child's Zone Presence
description: The notifications could directly identify the child's presence in specific geofenced zones, potentially revealing sensitive location information to unauthorized recipients.
assumptions: Notifications contain or can be correlated with child identity information.
uncertainty_note: Tree node I.1.1 is a general identification node; specific implementation details would affect exact classification.

title: Unauthorized Disclosure of Geofencing Data
description: The geofencing notifications could be disclosed to unauthorized parties during transmission to the ExternalEntity, potentially exposing the child's location patterns to third parties.
assumptions: Transmission channel may not be adequately secured or access controls may be insufficient.
uncertainty_note: Tree node D.1.1 is a general disclosure node; specific security controls would affect actual risk.

title: Usurpation of Notification System
description: An attacker could potentially impersonate the Geofencing Engine to send false arrival/departure notifications, misleading the parent about the child's actual location.
assumptions: Authentication mechanisms may be weak or absent, allowing unauthorized entities to send notifications.
uncertainty_note: Tree node U.1.1 is a general usurpation node; specific authentication controls would affect actual risk.

title: Parent-Child Profile Linkability
description: Parent's registration data can be linked to child's profile information (name, DOB, school, geofence zones), potentially enabling tracking of child's activities through parent's identity.
assumptions: System stores parent and child data in a way that allows correlation
uncertainty_note: Using L.1.1 as generic linkability node; specific LINDDUN Pro node may vary

title: Parent Identity Identification
description: Parent's identity is explicitly captured during account registration, creating identification risk if data is exposed or misused.
assumptions: Registration requires identifiable parent information
uncertainty_note: Using I.1.1 as generic identification node

title: Child Sensitive Data Disclosure
description: Child's sensitive profile data (name, DOB, school, geofence zones) could be disclosed to unauthorized parties through the registration flow.
assumptions: Child data is transmitted to backend during registration
uncertainty_note: Using D.1.1 as generic disclosure node

title: Parent Identity Usurpation
description: Malicious actor could usurp parent's identity to create unauthorized child profiles, potentially accessing or manipulating child data.
assumptions: Parent identity verification is not sufficiently robust
uncertainty_note: Using U.1.1 as generic usurpation node

title: Child Profile Data Alteration
description: Mobile App Backend process could alter child's profile data (name, DOB, school, geofence zones) maliciously or through bugs.
assumptions: Process has write access to child profile data
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 as generic data alteration node

title: Child Privacy Regulation Non-Compliance
description: Process may fail to comply with child privacy regulations (e.g., COPPA, GDPR-K) regarding collection and storage of child's personal data.
assumptions: System must comply with applicable child privacy laws
uncertainty_note: Using Nc.1.1 as generic non-compliance node

title: Excessive Personal Data Storage in Family Account Store
description: The backend (P1) stores comprehensive account, child profile, and geofence zone data in DS2. This raises concerns about data minimality - whether all stored data is strictly necessary for the intended functionality, or if some data could be collected/processed without compromising service quality.
assumptions: The system stores more data than minimally required for account management and geofencing functionality.
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 based on context [3] about data disclosure and minimality principle

title: Unauthorized Access to Stored Family Account Data
description: Personal data including child profiles and geofence zones stored in DS2 could be accessed by unauthorized parties if access controls are insufficient. This is particularly sensitive given the data involves minors.
assumptions: Access controls to DS2 may not be sufficiently restrictive or properly enforced.
uncertainty_note: U.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro node for unauthorized access

title: Data Integrity Risk for Child Profile Information
description: Child profile and geofence zone data stored in DS2 could be tampered with or corrupted, potentially leading to incorrect location tracking or safety concerns. Data integrity is critical for child safety applications.
assumptions: Inadequate integrity controls or encryption for data at rest in DS2.
uncertainty_note: D.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro node for data integrity threats

title: Identifiability of Stored Family Data
description: The combination of account data, child profiles, and geofence zones in DS2 could enable identification of specific individuals, particularly children, even if some fields are anonymized. The data is inherently identifiable.
assumptions: Stored data contains sufficient personally identifiable information to identify individuals.
uncertainty_note: I.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro node for identifiability threats

title: Linkability of Parent Identity to Child Location Data
description: An observer can link the parent's identity (EE1) to the child's location data being requested, potentially enabling tracking of the child's movements through the parent's access patterns.
assumptions: Parent's identity is identifiable in the request, and location data is associated with the child.

title: Identification of Child's Location
description: The location data transmitted to the parent (EE1) can be used to identify the child's current whereabouts or historical movements, potentially revealing sensitive patterns about the child's daily routine.
assumptions: Location data is precise enough to identify specific locations or patterns.

title: Unauthorized Disclosure of Location Data
description: The Mobile App Backend (P1) may disclose the child's location data to unauthorized parties through vulnerabilities, improper access controls, or data breaches.
assumptions: Location data is stored or transmitted in a way that could be intercepted or accessed by unauthorized entities.

title: Manipulation of Location Data
description: The Mobile App Backend (P1) could potentially alter or manipulate the location data before transmission, presenting false location information to the parent.
assumptions: The system lacks integrity controls or authentication mechanisms to prevent data tampering.

title: Usurpation of Parent Identity
description: An attacker could impersonate the parent (EE1) to gain unauthorized access to the child's location data through the Mobile App Backend (P1).
assumptions: Authentication mechanisms are weak or compromised, allowing identity spoofing.

title: Non-compliance with Location Privacy Regulations
description: The Mobile App Backend (P1) may fail to comply with privacy regulations (e.g., GDPR, COPPA) regarding the collection, processing, or disclosure of children's location data.
assumptions: The system does not implement adequate consent mechanisms, data minimization, or retention policies for children's data.

title: Location History Linkability to Parent Identity
description: Location history data retrieved by the backend can be linked to the parent's identity through the map/history view, potentially revealing movement patterns and associations with other data sources.
assumptions: The system does not adequately anonymize or pseudonymize location data before display.
uncertainty_note: Tree node L.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro node for linkability threats; exact node may vary by version.

title: Location History Enables Direct Identification
description: Location history data inherently contains identifying information about the parent's movements, routines, and locations, which can be used to identify the individual without additional authentication.
assumptions: Location data is not sufficiently aggregated or generalized before being served to the view.
uncertainty_note: Tree node I.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro node for identification threats; exact node may vary by version.

title: Unauthorized Disclosure of Location History
description: The backend process may disclose location history to unauthorized parties through improper access controls, logging, or data transmission vulnerabilities.
assumptions: Access controls and data transmission security are not fully implemented or are misconfigured.
uncertainty_note: Tree node D.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro node for disclosure threats; exact node may vary by version.

title: Usurpation of Location History Access
description: An attacker could impersonate the parent or exploit authentication weaknesses to access and view the location history that should be restricted to authorized users only.
assumptions: Authentication mechanisms may have vulnerabilities or the parent's identity is not properly verified before data retrieval.
uncertainty_note: Tree node U.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro node for usurpation threats; exact node may vary by version.

title: Parent-Child Location Linkability
description: The parent (EE1) could link their own identity with the child's location data through the invitation mechanism, potentially creating a profile that associates the parent with the child's movements.
assumptions: Parent has access to both their own and child's data
uncertainty_note: Using L.1.1 as a reasonable node for linkability at source

title: Parent Identification via Invitation
description: The parent's identity could be inferred or identified through the invitation process, potentially exposing their relationship to the child to unauthorized parties.
assumptions: Invitation metadata contains identifying information
uncertainty_note: Using I.1.1 as a reasonable node for identification at source

title: Unauthorized Guardian Access to Location Data
description: The mobile app backend (P1) could disclose the child's location data to the secondary guardian without proper authorization or consent verification.
assumptions: System lacks robust access controls for guardian data sharing
uncertainty_note: Using D.1.1 as a reasonable node for disclosure at destination

title: Excessive Location Data Collection
description: The mobile app backend (P1) may collect and store more location data than necessary for the secondary guardian viewing feature, violating data minimization principles.
assumptions: System collects historical or granular location data beyond what's needed
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 as a reasonable node for data minimization at destination

title: Guardian Identity Usurpation
description: An unauthorized party could impersonate a secondary guardian to access the child's location data through the mobile app backend (P1).
assumptions: Authentication mechanisms for guardian access are weak or bypassable
uncertainty_note: Using U.1.1 as a reasonable node for usurpation at destination

title: Location Flow Linkability
description: The data flow itself could be observed to link the parent (EE1) with the secondary guardian, revealing the relationship and potentially enabling tracking of the flow pattern.
assumptions: Network traffic or metadata could be intercepted
uncertainty_note: Using L.2.1 as a reasonable node for linkability at flow level

title: Flow Metadata Identification
description: Metadata about the data flow (e.g., source, destination, timing) could be used to identify the parent and secondary guardian's relationship and location-sharing behavior.
assumptions: Flow metadata is exposed or observable
uncertainty_note: Using I.2.1 as a reasonable node for identification at flow level

title: Identification of Child from Location Data
description: The secondary guardian (EE3) can identify the child's precise location and movements from the shared live location data, potentially enabling tracking and surveillance of the child's activities.
assumptions: The guardian has access to the location data and can correlate it with other information to identify the child.

title: Unauthorized Disclosure of Location Data
description: The secondary guardian may share or disclose the child's live location data to unauthorized third parties, violating the child's privacy expectations and potentially exposing them to risks.
assumptions: The guardian may have motives to share location data with others, and there are no technical or policy controls preventing this.

title: Linkability of Location Data with Other Information
description: The secondary guardian can link the child's location data with other personal information they may have access to, creating a comprehensive profile of the child's movements and habits.
assumptions: The guardian has access to additional data sources that can be correlated with the location data.

title: Regulatory Non-Compliance in Location Sharing
description: Sharing the child's live location with a secondary guardian may violate child privacy regulations (e.g., COPPA, GDPR-K) if proper consent mechanisms and data protection measures are not in place.
assumptions: The data sharing arrangement does not comply with applicable child privacy laws and regulations.

title: Linkability of Aggregated Analytics Data
description: Even though data is described as 'aggregated', there is a risk that usage and engagement patterns could be linked with other datasets (e.g., device IDs, IP addresses, or other partner data) to re-identify individual users or create detailed user profiles.
assumptions: Partner may have access to additional data sources that could be combined with this analytics data
uncertainty_note: Using L.1.1 as a reasonable node for linkability threats in Process→ExternalEntity flows

title: Unauthorized Disclosure to Third Parties
description: The advertising/analytics partner may share or sell the received analytics data to additional third parties beyond the original scope of the partnership, leading to unauthorized disclosure of user engagement information.
assumptions: Partner may have business incentives to monetize data beyond the agreed purpose
uncertainty_note: D.1.1 selected as representative disclosure threat node for Process→ExternalEntity flows

title: Excessive Data Collection and Sharing
description: The backend may share more detailed usage and engagement data than necessary for the stated advertising/analytics purpose, violating data minimization principles.
assumptions: The 'aggregated' description may not reflect actual data granularity being transmitted
uncertainty_note: Dd.1.1 used as representative data minimization node

title: Regulatory Non-Compliance in Third-Party Data Sharing
description: Sharing user analytics with external advertising partners may violate GDPR, CCPA, or other privacy regulations if proper consent mechanisms, data processing agreements, or user notification requirements are not in place.
assumptions: User consent for third-party analytics sharing may not be explicitly obtained or documented
uncertainty_note: Nc.1.1 selected as representative non-compliance node for external data sharing scenarios

title: Linkability of SOS message to specific child
description: The SOS message with location data can be linked to a specific child (EE2), enabling tracking of their movements and activities across multiple check-ins.
assumptions: The system stores historical check-in data and can correlate multiple messages to the same child.

title: Identifiability of child's location
description: The SOS message contains precise location data that can identify the child's current whereabouts, potentially revealing sensitive information about their daily routine or location patterns.
assumptions: Location data is transmitted with sufficient precision to identify specific places.

title: Unauthorized disclosure of location data
description: The child's location data from SOS messages could be disclosed to unauthorized parties (e.g., other family members, third-party services, or malicious actors) without proper consent or access controls.
assumptions: The system may share location data with multiple recipients or store it in accessible databases.

title: Excessive location data collection
description: The system may collect more location data than necessary for the SOS/check-in function, such as continuous tracking or historical location history beyond what's needed for emergency response.
assumptions: The system stores and processes location data beyond the immediate SOS message requirement.
